items.title: Tennessee RB Daune Morris breaks his leg in a car crash ahead of Texas A&M game
items.summary:
Tennessee running back Daune Morris sustained a broken leg in an early morning car crash, the school said Friday.

The crash comes ahead of No. 9 Tennessee’s game at Texas A&M on Saturday.

“Tennessee running back Daune Morris was involved in a one-vehicle accident off campus early Friday morning,” the school said in a statement. “He sustained non-life threatening injuries, including a broken leg, and is resting comfortably. We wish Daune the best in his recovery.”

Morris was ticketed for reckless driving following the crash, according to a police report. The report says the 19-year-old was driving a Dodge Charger with two passengers when he lost control and hit a fire hydrant and four parked cars in a parking lot before the Charger flipped and came to rest on its roof.

Morris was wearing a seat belt and no alcohol or drugs were involved, according to the police report. He was taken to the University of Tennessee Medical Center to be evaluated while his passengers declined medical treatment.

Last month, Morris was charged with misdemeanor charges of speeding and failure exercise due care as a driver after being pulled over for going 101 mph in a 65-mph zone, according to court records obtained by the Knoxville News Sentinel.

That incident came early in the morning after Tennessee’s win over Auburn on Oct. 3. He pleaded guilty to both charges and paid $507 in fines and court costs.

It is the Golden Knights (16-4-1) first sectional crown since 2022, when they were in Group 2. It was their second win over Ramapo (11-8-1) this season after edging the Green Raiders on penalty kicks in the Bergen County Tournament.

Playing with the wind at their back in the first half, Ramapo had possession early, but trailed 1-0 three minutes in when Pothos, who committed to Rutgers last month, took a short pass and ran 40 yards down the bench-side into the attacking zone. When she cut into the box, there was contact with a Ramapo defender, a whistle and she drilled the ensuing penalty kick low and to her right.

“It went a little more toward the middle than I wanted,” Pothos said. “But it worked out in my favor.”

items.title: Kirk Cousins will start against the Packers
items.summary:
(Photo by Elizabeth Flores/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images) As we all expected, the Minnesota Vikings will have Kirk Cousins under center on Sunday. Vikings head coach Kevin O’Connell announced the change in the lineup on Friday, just days after the team traded for Cousins from the Las Vegas Raiders.

Cousins was previously the Vikings’ starting quarterback from 2018 to 2023, which overlapped with O’Connell’s time there. On Wednesday, Packers head coach Matt LaFleur stated that the team expected Cousins to start for Minnesota.

For what it’s worth, the Vikings didn’t have a practice on Wednesday, as they were coming off a short turnaround from Monday Night Football , but did on Thursday and Friday. That MNF game featured an 8-of-25 performance from injury-replacement starter Carson Wentz, ultimately boiling down to an 8.9 passer rating — which prompted the trade for Cousins.

In other news, O’Connell also stated that linebacker Blake Cashman (concussion) and tight end T.J. Hockenson (wrist/chest) won’t play on Sunday. Receiver Jordan Addison and nickelback Josh Metellus were injured on Friday and have been listed as questionable by the Vikings.

items.title: DeMarvion Overshown's penalty raises question of whether Cowboys have discipline problem
items.summary:
FRISCO, Texas (AP) — DeMarvion Overshown said he didn't know inactive players in street clothes couldn't run on the field to celebrate before committing the 14th and final penalty by the Dallas Cowboys last weekend.

Whether the linebacker nursing hamstring and back injuries should have known — and whether it's emblematic of a discipline problem under Brian Schottenheimer and his staff — went unanswered by the second-year coach.

The Cowboys got a game-winning drive from Dak Prescott to beat the Indianapolis Colts 27-23 despite all kinds of mistakes, but the reality is Dallas (4-5) is either finding ways to lose, or making things much harder than necessary with rampant miscues, heading into a meeting with NFC-leading San Francisco (7-1) on Sunday.

The image of Overshown chasing down his celebrating defensive teammates after a fumble recovery was startling. Then there was referee Clay Martin's explanation of the unsportsmanlike conduct penalty: “We had a nonuniformed player in blue sweats and a stocking cap come onto the field to celebrate.”

The Cowboys lost 15 yards of field position when trying to protect a three-point lead in the fourth quarter, and ended up with 153 yards in penalties, leaving them with an NFL-leading 667 for the season.

“I feel like that's what made it worse,” Overshown said Thursday. “We already had 13, 14 penalties, then getting one from a guy that's not even playing, it's like, ‘What are we doing?’ I wouldn't say that's part of an undisciplined team. That's just me not being aware of what's going on. That's not an indictment on (Schottenheimer)…

The Test captain kept his promise to answer all questions at a press conference that made his position clear and filled some but not all gaps

Our coverage on Thursday said that Pat Cummins needed to front up, and nobody can fairly say that he didn’t. It was a proper ’til-they-drop affair from Australia’s cricket captain, an hour and eight minutes at a press conference podium taking questions about the 2018 ball-tampering episode until every journalist present ran out of steam. You might have expected some partial concession to teammate Usman Khawaja’s depiction of endemic cheating, but Cummins was firm that this did not reflect the life he’d known. Once more with feeling, but more importantly with detail.

Media accounts will now depict this as Cummins and Khawaja at war, because a falling-out among friends is a juicy story to fatten up and serve for gluttony. It isn’t fair, because both have emphasised the importance of their friendship, strained as it must now be. As two thoughtful people with shared history, they have a better chance than most to find a way through.

items.title: The beautiful game: revived art prize gives football its creative due once more | Emma John
items.summary:
Football and the art world have long remained distant but the breadth of entries for this year’s award reveals a healthy revival

It may be the Beautiful Game, but in its early decades football was a rare subject for artists. The Italian Futurist Umberto Boccioni whirled an athlete’s body into a vortex of movement in his 1913 painting Dynamism of a Soccer Player. You can see one of the earliest fine art depictions of a match – a smoggy, factory-adjactent scene called Any Wintry Afternoon in England – at the Manchester Art Gallery. If 1930s abstraction is more your thing, you can enjoy decoding the geometric shapes in Kazimir Malevich’s Painterly Realism of a Football Player – Color Masses in the 4th Dimension. I’m guessing the small green pea shape is a ball.

These, in any case, were exceptions. In 1953 the Football Association launched an art prize, backed by the newly formed Arts Council: the winning works included Going To The Match by LS Lowry, with its crowds flocking to Bolton Wanderers’ then home ground, Burnden Park. An exhibition of the submissions, Football and The Fine Arts, toured the country and the FA secretary, Sir Stanley Rous, said he hoped it would finally break the barrier between those two worlds.

items.title: It’s Happy Harry Kane day as England’s finest seizes his moment in style | Barney Ronay

The Ballon d’Or validated the forward’s career and he extended his incredible record for England with yet another goal on his 126th appearance

Happy Harry Kane day! And many happy Harry returns. There is a process in clinical psychology known as semantic satiation. Subjects are asked to repeat a word or phrase so many times that it loses any kind of meaning. Suddenly “daffodils” is just an absurd, empty set of sounds. So it was in the buildup to Harry Kane’s record-breaking 126th cap, at the end of Harry Kane Ballon d’Or fortnight, as Harry Kane’s England were led out by top scorer Harry Kane, climax to a week of Harry Kane tributes, Harry Kane montages, 26-page Harry Kane … wait. Where were we?

This was that kind of occasion from start to finish, a night where you expected to look up from your desk mid-match to see Kane’s head looming helpfully over your shoulder, to enter the Wembley toilets at half-time and find him silently offering you a breath mint and a scented tissue.
